Creating a video editor is one of the best hard projects you can take on - it's part media engineering, part graphics programming, part product design.

Here's the full blueprint to build it yourself, without any code.

Phase 1: Define What You're Building First

Don't try to build Premiere on day one. Pick your lane:

1. Scope:

  • What platform? Desktop (Windows/Mac/Linux), Web-based, or Mobile?
  • What type of editor? Simple trimmer/cutter like CapCut, full NLE like DaVinci Resolve, or template-based like Canva Video?
  • MVP features: Start with this set: Import > Timeline > Cut/Trim > Transitions > Text > Audio layer > Export 1080p. Everything else is Phase 2.

2. Product Research:

  • Use 5 editors deeply: DaVinci Resolve, CapCut, Premiere Pro, Kdenlive (open source), and Shotcut. Note their timeline interaction, how they handle previews, and export dialogs.
  • Decide on your differentiator. Is it speed? AI features? Lightweight for low-end PCs? That decides your architecture.

Phase 2: The Core Concepts You MUST Understand

This is the theory that makes or breaks your editor.

1. Video Fundamentals:

  • Containers vs Codecs: Container = .mp4, .mov, .mkv (the box). Codec = h.264, h.265, VP9, AV1 (how video/audio inside is compressed). You need to demux the container and decode the codec.
  • Frames, FPS, and Timebase: Video is not time in seconds, it's time in frames. All your logic should work on a timebase (e.g., PTS - Presentation Timestamp). 30fps vs 60fps handling will break you if you use seconds.
  • Color Spaces: YUV vs RGB, 8-bit vs 10-bit, HDR. Your preview will look washed out if you ignore this.
  • Audio: Sample rate, audio mixing, waveform generation.

2. The Non-Linear Editing (NLE) Engine - The Heart:

  • Timeline Model: This is NOT linear. You need a data structure for Tracks (V1, V2, A1, A2...), Clips on tracks with start time, duration, in-point, out-point.
  • Project File: How you save the edit. Usually JSON/XML that stores references to media, not the media itself.
  • Compositing & Layering: How V2 overlays V1. Concept of alpha channel, blend modes.
  • Transform Stack: Every clip has properties that change over time: Position, Scale, Rotation, Opacity, Volume. These need Keyframes and interpolation (linear, bezier).

3. Playback and Rendering:

  • Decode -> Filter -> Composite -> Encode Pipeline: This is the universal pipeline. You decode raw frames -> apply effects/transforms -> composite all tracks into one frame -> send to preview OR to encoder.
  • Real-time Preview vs Export: Preview needs to be fast, so you use low-res proxies and drop frames. Export needs to be accurate, so you render every frame.
  • Hardware Acceleration: Decoding and encoding on CPU is too slow. You must learn how to use GPU: NVENC / QuickSync / AMF for encoding, and GPU shaders (OpenGL/Vulkan/Metal/DirectX) for effects and compositing.

Phase 3: Architecture - How to Build It

Build it in this exact order. Don't skip steps.

Step 1: The Media Core
Choose your decoding backend. Don't write your own codec.

  • Industry standard: FFmpeg libraries (libavformat, libavcodec). It handles 99% of formats.
  • Alternative: GStreamer or MLT Framework (what Kdenlive and Shotcut use - highly recommended to study).
    Goal: Be able to load a video file and get its raw frames and metadata.

Step 2: The Timeline Engine (No UI yet)
Build a headless engine that can take your timeline data structure and for a given timestamp t, produce one composited frame + mixed audio sample.
Test it by exporting a simple edit without any UI.

Step 3: The Preview Player
Build the player that shows frames. This is where performance matters.

  • Concepts: Frame cache, Proxy workflow (create low-res versions for editing), Audio/Video sync.
  • You will need a windowing toolkit: For Desktop - Qt, Electron, or Tauri are common. For Web - Canvas + WebCodecs + WebAssembly.

Step 4: The UI / UX Layer

  • Media Bin: Where imports live.
  • Timeline UI: Drag-drop, snapping, ripple trim, razor cut, zoom. This is the hardest UI to get right.
  • Preview Canvas: With safe margins, overlays.
  • Properties & Effects Panel: Keyframe curve editor.
  • Keep UI on a separate thread from the rendering engine. Never block playback with UI work.

Step 5: Effects & Transitions
Start with CPU filters, then move to GPU shaders.

  • Essential: Transform, Crop, Opacity, Speed ramp, Color correction (LUTs), Blur, Chroma Key.
  • Transitions are just effects that take two clips as input: Cross-dissolve, Wipe.

Step 6: Export Engine

  • Muxing and encoding. User picks Resolution, FPS, Codec, Bitrate.
  • Handle progress, estimated time, and failure recovery.

Phase 4: What to Learn / Tech Stack to Evaluate

  • For Desktop Native (Best Performance): C++ or Rust + FFmpeg + Qt + OpenGL/Vulkan. Look at how Kdenlive does it - it's open source.
  • For Web-Based (Easiest Distribution): TypeScript + FFmpeg.wasm + WebCodecs API + WebGL for effects. Check how CapCut web works.
  • For Cross-Platform Quick MVP: Python with PyQt + MLT Framework bindings. Very fast to prototype.

Key Tools to Study (not copy code, just architecture):

  1. FFmpeg documentation - your bible
  2. MLT Framework docs - shows how professional timeline is built
  3. OpenTimelineIO by Pixar - standard for timeline interchange

A Practical Roadmap For You:

Month 1: MVP Cutter
Can import 1 video, cut it on a timeline, export it. No effects.

Month 2: Multi-Track
Add 2 video tracks + 1 audio track + text + image overlay. Add proxy preview.

Month 3: Polish
Add keyframes, transitions, color correction, proper audio mixing, and a stable project save file.

Pro tip: The #1 reason custom editors fail is sync. From day one, build your entire engine around a single master clock and make audio the master. If audio drifts, everything feels broken.

Perfect. Since you're starting mobile-first in Python, and you want the PC version to run on literally anything - Vista to Win 11, 1GB to 16GB RAM, iGPU or dedicated - your approach has to be different from a normal editor.

That Swaroop One-Shot course you watched covers you till: variables, data types, lists/tuples/dicts, if-else, loops, functions, import, OOP basics - classes, objects. That's enough to start. Now we build the editor using those same concepts.

MOBILE FIRST - How to do it in Python

Python doesn't run natively on Android. For mobile you need a bridge.

Your Mobile Stack:

  1. UI Framework: Kivy / KivyMD - This is your best option. It lets you write Python and package it as an Android APK. Alternatives like Flet or BeeWare are too slow for video.
  2. Packager: Buildozer - It takes your Kivy code and makes the APK.
  3. Video Engine: You CANNOT edit video with pure Python, it will be 100x too slow on mobile. You will use FFmpeg as a separate binary and call it from Python. Python is just the manager, FFmpeg does the heavy lifting.

Steps for Mobile Version:

Step 1: Learn the missing Python concepts [2-3 days]
From that course you need to go one level deeper:

  • threading - Because if you run FFmpeg on the main thread, your app will freeze. UI on one thread, export on another.
  • os, pathlib, subprocess - To manage video files and run FFmpeg commands.
  • OOP properly - You will design your editor as classes. Example: class Clip, class Track, class Timeline. A Timeline has a list of Tracks, a Track has a list of Clips. That's just lists inside classes you already know.

Step 2: Build the Core Engine WITHOUT UI
Don't start with UI. Make a folder my_editor_core and make it work in terminal first.

  • Make it able to: import video -> get info, trim video from 2s to 5s, add 2 videos together, add audio over video.
  • This engine will just build the correct FFmpeg command internally. Test it on your PC first.

Step 3: Build the Mobile UI
Now create Kivy app with 4 screens only for MVP:

  • 1. Gallery Screen: Show videos from phone storage. Simple file list.
  • 2. Timeline Screen: This is the hardest. For mobile, don't make Premiere-style timeline at first. Make it vertical list: Clip 1 -> Clip 2 -> Clip 3. Each item has Trim and Delete buttons. That's it.
  • 3. Preview Screen: Use Kivy's Video widget. It can't show real-time effects, so show original clip + "effect applied" as text. Real preview comes after export.
  • 4. Export Screen: Progress bar, quality selection (480p, 720p for mobile).

Step 4: Connect Engine + UI + Performance
Mobile phones have low RAM. You MUST implement:

  • Proxy Editing: When user imports a 4K video, create a small 480p copy for editing. Export uses the original 4K.
  • No real-time effects: On mobile, don't try to show filters live. Apply them only at export time. Otherwise app will crash on 2GB RAM phones.

PC VERSION - Universal Windows [Vista, 7, 8, 10, 11 with any RAM]

Your idea of "run on any PC" is smart but Python has a big problem here:

  • Python 3.9+ does NOT support Windows 7 or Vista.
  • Python 3.8 is the last version that supports Windows 7.
  • Windows Vista only supports Python 3.4.

So for universal support, you have to do this:

1. Use Python 3.8, 32-bit version.
32-bit runs on both 32-bit and 64-bit Windows, and uses less RAM. Perfect for 1GB RAM PCs.

2. Never rely on GPU.
You said iGPU or dedicated GPU - many 1GB PCs have no proper GPU driver. So:

  • All effects and compositing must have a CPU fallback. Use OpenGL for preview if available, but if not, fallback to software rendering.
  • For export, don't use NVENC. Use libx264 CPU encoding. It's slower but works everywhere.

3. Bundle everything.
Don't ask user to install FFmpeg or Python. Use PyInstaller to make a single .exe that includes Python 3.8 + FFmpeg 32-bit binary + your code. One file, double-click runs on Vista to Win 11.

4. RAM Management for 1GB PCs:

  • Never load full video in RAM. Always work with file references.
  • Clear cache after every preview.
  • Limit timeline resolution to 720p max for low RAM PCs. You can detect RAM with Python's psutil and auto-switch to low quality mode.

Your Correct Order of Work

Phase 1 - Mobile MVP [3-4 weeks]
Import -> List Timeline -> Trim -> Merge -> Export 720p

Phase 2 - Mobile Beta
Add Text, Music overlay, Speed control

Phase 3 - PC Universal
Take the same core engine from mobile, but make a new UI with Tkinter or PyQt5 [Qt works on Win7]. Tkinter is lighter for 1GB RAM, PyQt5 looks better.

Do NOT try to make mobile and PC UI in one codebase at start. Keep core engine same, UI different.

Biggest warning: A video editor is not just Python. 80% of work is FFmpeg knowledge and managing threads so app doesn't freeze.

I won't give you any code. Just what to do, in exact order. Follow this like a checklist.

LEVEL 0: Foundation - What you need BEFORE touching video editor

You know Python basics, but for an app you are missing 4 beginner concepts. Learn these first, 3 days max.

1. File and Folder Handling [1 day]
You need to understand how Python sees files. A video is just a file.
Learn: os, pathlib, shutil
Your task: Make a small practice project - a program that goes into a folder, finds all .mp4 files, and renames them. If you can do this, you can build a Gallery Screen later.

2. Running other programs from Python [1 day]
Your Python app will NOT edit video itself. It will tell another program called FFmpeg to edit it. This concept is called subprocess.
Learn: How to use subprocess module.
Your task: Make Python run a simple command like creating a folder or copying a file. This is how you will later tell FFmpeg to trim a video.

3. Threading - Most Important [1 day]
If you don't learn this, your app will freeze.
Imagine: Your UI is one person, Export is another person. If same person does both, UI freezes until export finishes. So you need 2 people working at same time. That's threading.
Learn: threading module basics.
Your task: Make a program with a button that starts a 10-second counting, and while counting, you can still type in another input box. If it freezes, you did it wrong.

4. What is FFmpeg? [1 day]
Download FFmpeg on your PC. It's just a .exe file.
Search YouTube: "FFmpeg basics trim cut merge"
Your task: Learn to trim a video using FFmpeg in Command Prompt / Terminal. Don't use Python yet, just CMD. If you can trim a video from CMD, your Python program can do the same.

LEVEL 1: Mobile Setup - How Python becomes an Android App

Step 1: Install Kivy
Kivy is a Python library that lets you make Android apps with buttons, video player, file lists.
Install it on PC and make 3 small dummy apps first:
a) App with 1 button that shows "Hello"
b) App that shows a video
c) App that lists files from a folder

If you can make these 3, you know 80% of what you need for UI.

Step 2: Understand Buildozer
Buildozer is what converts your Kivy Python code into an APK file for Android.
You need Linux for this. Use WSL on Windows or use Google Colab. Watch: "How to build Kivy APK with Buildozer"
Your task: Build your "Hello" app into APK and install on your phone. First APK is always hard, after that it's easy.

LEVEL 2: Now Build Your Editor - Exact Order

Don't try to build full editor. Build like this, one floor at a time.

Floor 1: The Brain [Most Important]
Make a new Python file called engine.py. This file has NO UI.
Make 3 Classes in it using the OOP you learned:

  • class VideoClip: It stores info of one video - where is the file, start time, end time.
  • class Track: It is a list that holds many VideoClips.
  • class Timeline: It holds many Tracks.

This is your project data. Everything else will use this.

Floor 2: Gallery
In Kivy, make a screen that shows all videos from phone's DCIM folder. When user clicks a video, you create a VideoClip object and add it to your Timeline.

Floor 3: Simple Timeline UI
Don't make a fancy timeline like Premiere. For beginner, make it simple:
Vertical list:
[ Clip 1 - Trim - Delete ]
[ Clip 2 - Trim - Delete ]
[ Clip 3 - Trim - Delete ]
That's it. This is your editor for now.

Floor 4: Trim Feature
When user clicks Trim on Clip 1, ask for start and end time. Then use your engine.py to call FFmpeg to make a new trimmed video file. Replace old clip with new one.

Floor 5: Preview
Add a Video Player widget in Kivy that plays whatever is selected in your timeline. This will be slow at first, that's normal.

Floor 6: Export Final Video
This is merging. Take all clips in your Timeline list, and tell FFmpeg to join them one by one into one final video. This is your first working version! It can import, trim, join, export.

After this, your V1 is ready.

LEVEL 3: After V1 - What to Add Next

Only after Floor 6 works, add these one by one:

  1. Add Text - It's just telling FFmpeg to add text on top of video
  2. Add Music - Mix 2 tracks: video audio + music audio
  3. Filters - Black & white, blur
  4. Speed - Fast / Slow motion

For Your Universal Windows Version Later

You said you want it to work on Vista, Win 7, 8, 10, 11 with 1GB RAM and any GPU.

For that you must remember 3 rules:
Rule 1: Use Python 3.8 32-bit only. Newer Python doesn't work on Win7/Vista.
Rule 2: Don't use GPU. Code everything to work on CPU only. On 1GB RAM PC, GPU effects will crash. Make a setting: If RAM < 2GB, automatically use 480p preview.
Rule 3: Make one .exe file with everything inside. User should not install Python or FFmpeg. Use tool called PyInstaller for this.

  2. Tomorrow: Make the file-renaming program and the threading practice program.
  3. Day 3: Install Kivy and make Hello app.
  4. Day 4: Build that Hello app into APK.

DAY 1: FFmpeg - How to trim video without Python

Goal: You will trim a video using only Command Prompt. If you can do this, Python can do it later.

Steps:

  1. Go to Google, search FFmpeg download Windows
  2. Open first site ffmpeg.org, go to Download. Download the Windows build with essentials build. It will be a zip file.
  3. Extract that zip. Inside you will find a folder called bin. Inside bin there is ffmpeg.exe. This is your video editor engine.
  4. Copy that ffmpeg.exe file and paste it on your Desktop for easy access.
  5. Now take any small video file from your phone, copy it to Desktop too. Rename it to input.mp4 to make it easy.
  6. On Desktop, hold SHIFT + Right Click, you will see Open in Terminal or Open Command Window Here. Click it. A black window will open.
  7. Now you have to learn 1 command. Search YouTube: ffmpeg trim video command. You will learn the command is something with -ss for start time, -to for end time, -i for input, and output name.
  8. Try it. Your goal is to make a new video called output.mp4 which is only 5 seconds from your input video.
  9. If output.mp4 is created and plays only 5 seconds, Day 1 DONE.

What you learned: How video cutting actually works behind the scenes.

DAY 2: Two Practice Projects - File Manager + Threading

Goal 1: File Manager Project
You learned list, for loop, os in that video, but you didn't use it.

  1. Create a new folder on Desktop called TestVideos. Put 5 dummy videos or photos inside.
  2. Your task: Make a Python program that opens that folder, sees all files inside, and prints their names.
  3. Search in Google: python os list files in folder - you will find the concept. Don't copy full code, just understand the function name.
  4. Next level of same task: Now make it rename all files. Like video1.mp4 to my_video_1.mp4. Use what you learned about for loop and os.rename.
  5. If this works, you have built your future Gallery Screen logic.

Goal 2: Threading Project
This is to stop your app from freezing.

  1. Search Google: python threading simple example for beginner
  2. Understand this idea: You have main program and you create a second program that runs at same time.
  3. Your task: Make a Python program that does this:
    • It asks user for input: "Enter your name"
    • At the SAME TIME, in background, it should keep printing numbers 1,2,3,4... every second.
  4. If you do it without threading, when it asks for name, number counting will stop. That's called freezing.
  5. With threading, counting should continue even while it waits for your name.
  6. When you achieve that - where input box works AND counting happens in background - Day 2 DONE.

You have learned how to keep UI alive while export happens.

DAY 3: Kivy - Make Your First Mobile App on PC

Goal: Make an Android-like app but run it on your PC first.

  1. Open Command Prompt. Search how to install kivy. You will find command pip install kivy. Run it.
  2. Installation takes time. Wait.
  3. Now search YouTube: Kivy hello world app tutorial. Watch only first 10 minutes. Don't watch full video editor tutorial.
  4. You will understand Kivy has 2 parts: Python file for logic, and a design part for buttons.
  5. Your Task 1: Make an app that has only ONE button in center saying "Hello". When you press it, it should print something in console. Run it on PC. If it opens a window with button, success.
  6. Your Task 2: Make second app - App with a button Pick Video and a Label below it that says No video selected. When you click Pick Video, label should change to Video selected. This teaches you how button changes UI. This will be your future import button.
  7. Your Task 3: Search kivy video player example. Make third app that plays your input.mp4 from Day 1 inside the app window.
  8. If 3 apps work on PC, Day 3 DONE. Don't try to build APK yet.

DAY 4: Build APK - Put Your App on Your Phone

This is the hardest day. Follow slowly.

  1. You cannot build APK on Windows easily. You need Linux. Best way for beginners: Use WSL.
  2. Search: How to install WSL on Windows 10. It's one command. Install Ubuntu from Microsoft Store.
  3. Open Ubuntu. It looks like Command Prompt but it's Linux.
  4. Inside Ubuntu, search how to install buildozer. Install Buildozer and its dependencies. This step is long, many commands, but just follow one tutorial fully. Search buildozer install ubuntu 2024.
  5. Now take your simplest Hello Button app from Day 3 - copy its Python file into Ubuntu folder.
  6. In Ubuntu, inside your app folder, run buildozer init. It will create a file called buildozer.spec. Open it.
  7. Inside that file you have to change 3 things only: App name, package name, and orientation. Watch video: buildozer.spec explained.
  8. Now run buildozer -v android debug. This will download many things for first time - 1 hour or more. Keep PC on charging, internet on. Don't close.
  9. If no error, at the end you will find a file yourapp-0.1-debug.apk in bin folder.
  10. Copy that APK to your Android phone, install it. If your Hello button app opens on phone, you have WON. You are now a mobile app developer.

Day 4 is complete when your app runs on phone.

After Day 4, you have everything:

  • You know how to cut video [Day 1]
  • You know how to manage files and threading [Day 2]
  • You know how to make mobile UI [Day 3]
  • You know how to make APK [Day 4]

From Day 5, you will combine all 4 days and start your real editor.

Yes, here is the exact steps for Windows 7 - step by step.

How to Download FFmpeg for Windows 7

Step 1: Go to correct website

  1. Open Chrome / Firefox
  2. Search in Google: gyan.dev ffmpeg builds
  3. Click the first link that says gyan.dev - FFmpeg Builds

Why this site? The official ffmpeg.org site is confusing for beginners. gyan.dev gives you ready .zip file for Windows.

Step 2: Download

  1. On that page, you will see 2 versions: ffmpeg-git-essentials and ffmpeg-git-full
  2. You download ffmpeg-git-essentials.zip - This is small and enough for you.
  3. Click it, downloading will start. File size around 80-100 MB.

If gyan.dev site not opening, search ffmpeg windows build by BtbN and download from his GitHub releases. Same zip.

Step 3: Extract

  1. After download, go to Downloads folder. You will see ffmpeg-git-essentials.zip
  2. Right click on it -> Extract All or Extract Here. If you don't have extractor, install WinRAR or 7-Zip first.
  3. After extract, you will get a folder. Name will be like ffmpeg-...-essentials_build
  4. Open that folder -> Open folder called bin inside it.
  5. Inside bin you will see 3 files: ffmpeg.exe, ffplay.exe, ffprobe.exe
  6. ffmpeg.exe is your main video editor. Don't delete others, keep them.

Step 4: Make it easy to use
For beginner, do this easy method - don't add to PATH now:

  1. Make a new folder on Desktop. Name it MyVideoEditor
  2. Copy all 3 exe files from that bin folder and PASTE them into MyVideoEditor folder on Desktop.
  3. Now also copy any small test video file into SAME MyVideoEditor folder. Rename that video to input.mp4

Now your folder has: ffmpeg.exe, ffplay.exe, ffprobe.exe, input.mp4

Step 5: Test if it works

  1. Inside MyVideoEditor folder, click on address bar at top where it shows C:\Users\...\Desktop\MyVideoEditor
  2. Type cmd and press Enter. A black window will open, already inside your folder.
  3. In black window, type this and press Enter:
    ffmpeg -version
  4. If it shows some text like ffmpeg version ... then FFmpeg is working.
  5. If it says not recognized, you are not inside correct folder. Close and try again from Step 5.1.

Step 6: Your first cut test
In same black window, after ffmpeg -version worked, type:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -ss 00:00:02 -to 00:00:07 -c copy output.mp4

Press Enter.

What this means:

  • -i input.mp4 = your original video
  • -ss 00:00:02 = start from 2nd second
  • -to 00:00:07 = end at 7th second
  • output.mp4 = new video name

After it finishes, you will see output.mp4 in same folder. Double click and play. It should be 5 seconds long.

If output.mp4 is created, you have successfully installed FFmpeg.

Common Problem on Windows 7:
If double-clicking ffmpeg.exe and it closes immediately, that's NORMAL. ffmpeg.exe is not supposed to be double-clicked. You must run it from black CMD window only, like we did in Step 5.

Goal 2: Threading - Stop App Freezing [Evening]

This is very important for your mobile editor.

  1. Create new file thread_test.py on Desktop
  2. Understand the problem first WITHOUT threading:
    • Make a program that does:
    • First, ask user Enter your name:
    • Then, start counting 1 to 10 with 1 second delay between each number
    • You will see: It waits for your name FIRST, only after you enter name, counting starts. That's freezing!
  3. Now learn threading:
    • Search Google: python threading example beginner
    • Understand: You can make counting run in a separate thread
  4. Your task WITH threading:
    • Make counting 1 to 10 happen in background thread
    • At same time, main program asks Enter your name:
    • Result: Counting should continue printing numbers EVEN WHILE it's waiting for you to type your name!
    • If counting doesn't stop while you are typing, you learned threading!
  5. This is exactly what will happen in your editor: Export runs in background thread, UI stays alive.

Let me explain what Google gave you, in simple words, because you know these concepts from Swaroop video.

What is import os ?

os means Operating System. It's a Python library that lets Python talk to Windows. Like "Hey Windows, show me files in this folder". Without import os, Python cannot see files.

You learned import in Swaroop video - same concept.

Now your 3 examples - which one to use?

Example 2 - This is for you as beginner - START WITH THIS ONE:

Python
import osfolder_path = "path/to/your/folder"all_contents = os.listdir(folder_path)

What it does:

  • folder_path = Where is your folder? Like address. You have to change "path/to/your/folder" to your real folder address. Example: C:\Users\abcd PC\Desktop\TestVideos
  • os.listdir(folder_path) = Go to that folder and make a LIST of everything inside. Remember list from Swaroop video? Same list! It will have names like ["a.mp4", "b.mp4", "c.mp4"]
  • print(all_contents) = Show that list

This is your first task - Just make this work with your TestVideos folder.

Example 1 - Next level - After you do Example 2:

Python
files = [    f    for f in os.listdir(folder_path)    if os.path.isfile(os.path.join(folder_path, f))]

This is list comprehension - Swaroop also taught this quickly.

What extra it does:

  • os.path.isfile = Check if it is a FILE or FOLDER. Because os.listdir shows both files and folders. You only want files, not folders.
  • So it says: "Give me only those items which are files, not folders"

You need this later because inside TestVideos you might have folders also.

Example 3 - For later - Filter only .mp4 or .txt

Python
if f.endswith(".txt")

This checks: Does file name end with .txt?
You will change .txt to .mp4 for your video editor! So it will show only mp4 files, not all files.

  • for file in all_contents: - take one file at a time from your big list
  • if file.endswith(".mp4"): - check if that file ends with .mp4
  • video_files.append(file) - if yes, add it to new list
  • print(video_files) - print only mp4 list AFTER loop finishes

can u explain how a pc renames a file using a code?
Today
Show thinking

Great question! This is exactly what your os.rename is doing behind the scenes.

Forget code for a minute, think how Windows 7 actually stores a file.

How PC stores a file - Library example

Imagine your TESTVIDEOS folder is a library room.

  1. Inside the room, there is a big table at entrance. This table is called Directory Table. Windows calls it MFT on NTFS.

  2. On that table, there are rows:

Code
Row 1: Name = "BMW M4.jpg" -> Points to shelf number 105Row 2: Name = "gallery.py" -> Points to shelf number 210
  1. The actual file data (the photo, the video) is NOT on the table. It's on the shelves (your Hard Disk / 256GB storage). The table only has the name and the address of where the data is.

So what happens when you rename a file with code?

When your Python code says rename old name to new name, this happens:

Step 1: Python -> Windows
Your Python program doesn't touch the hard disk directly. It tells Windows: "Hey Windows, please rename this file for me". This is called a System Call.

Step 2: Windows checks
Windows checks: Does old file exist? Does new name already exist? Do you have permission to rename? You have Windows 7 with your user abcd PC, so yes you have permission in Desktop folder.

Step 3: Windows changes ONLY the table, not the data
Windows goes to that big Directory Table and just erases old name and writes new name, but keeps same shelf number!

Before rename:
{{IE_30000}}BMW{{/IE_30000}} M4.jpg -> shelf 105

After rename:
BMW_M4.jpg -> shelf 105

See? The photo data on shelf 105 never moved, never copied, never changed. Only the name label on the table changed. That's why renaming is instant - even if file is 3GB, rename takes 0.001 second. Because Windows doesn't move data.

Step 4: Windows tells Python
Windows tells Python: "Done". Then your Python program continues.

Why this matters for your video editor?

This is why your Gallery filter is so fast.

When you did os.listdir, Windows just read that table and gave you names. It didn't open the actual videos.

And when you will build your editor, you will NEVER rename or move the original video file itself. You will create a NEW output file with FFmpeg. Original input.mp4 stays safe.

If renaming actually moved data on hard disk, your 4GB RAM PC with iGPU would become very slow!

So to remember:
Renaming = Changing label on table, not moving the book.

Does this make sense? Want me to explain how os.listdir works the same way - how PC lists files without opening them?

PERFECT! You found the exact problem every Windows 7 iGPU PC has!

Look at your error:
GL: Minimum required OpenGL version (2.0) NOT FOUND!
OpenGL version detected: 1.1
Renderer: GDI Generic

This means your iGPU graphics driver is not installed properly. Windows 7 is using Microsoft's basic driver GDI Generic which only has OpenGL 1.1, but Kivy needs OpenGL 2.0.

This is exactly why you said you want your PC editor to work on any graphics driver - iGPU or dedicated! You are now facing the same problem your future users will face!

Fix for your Windows 7 iGPU - 2 options:

Option 1 - Try to force Kivy to use DirectX instead of OpenGL [Fastest - Try this first]:

Your Kivy already installed kivy-deps.angle which can convert OpenGL to DirectX - DirectX works on your iGPU!

Do this - Change your main.py to this:

At the very top, add 2 lines BEFORE from kivy.app import App:

import osos.environ['KIVY_GL_BACKEND'] = 'angle_sdl2'from kivy.app import Appfrom kivy.uix.button import Button

How to Convert Python File to .EXE App - For Universal Windows

Step 1: Install PyInstaller - The App Maker

  1. Open black CMD window - Hold SHIFT + Right Click inside MyFirstApp folder -> Open command window here
  2. Type this and press Enter:
    pip install pyinstaller
  3. Wait 2-3 minutes till it says Successfully installed pyinstaller

Step 2: Build Your App

In same black window, inside MyFirstApp folder, type this command and press Enter:

pyinstaller --onefile --windowed --name "MyVideoEditorUniversal" main_tk.py

What this means:

  • --onefile = Make ONE single .exe file, not many files
  • --windowed = Don't show black console window, only show your app window
  • --name "MyVideoEditorUniversal" = Name of your final app
  • main_tk.py = Your Python file

Step 3: Wait - Takes 2-3 minutes

You will see many lines like Analyzing..., Building.... Don't close.

On your 4GB RAM PC, it will take 2-3 minutes.

Step 4: Find Your .EXE App!

  1. After it finishes, go to your MyFirstApp folder
  2. You will see 2 new folders created: build and dist
  3. Open dist folder
  4. Inside dist, you will see: MyVideoEditorUniversal.exe - THIS IS YOUR APP!

Step 5: Test Your App Like a Real User

  1. Copy that MyVideoEditorUniversal.exe to Desktop
  2. Double-click it!
  3. Your same window should open: My Video Editor - Universal with button Hello - My Editor - Works Anywhere!

But now it's NOT Python file - It's a real Windows app! No need to type python main_tk.py anymore!

This .exe will work on:

  • Windows Vista, 7, 8, 10, 11
  • 1GB, 2GB, 4GB, 8GB, 16GB RAM
  • iGPU or Dedicated GPU
  • Even if Python and FFmpeg are NOT installed on that PC! Because PyInstaller puts Python inside the .exe!

CODE for main_tk.py - Replace your old code with this:

Python
import osimport sysimport subprocessimport tkinter as tkfrom tkinter import filedialog

MEANING OF EVERY WORD - Line by Line:

Line 1: import os

  • import = Bring a tool/library from Python into your file. You learned this in Swaroop video.
  • os = Operating System tool. Lets you talk to Windows - get file names, file paths, join paths.

Line 2: import sys

  • sys = System tool. Tells you "Am I running as normal Python file or as .exe app made by PyInstaller?". Needed to find ffmpeg.exe inside .exe.

Line 3: import subprocess

  • subprocess = Tool to run other programs from Python. You will use it to run ffmpeg.exe command like you did in black CMD window.

Line 4: import tkinter as tk

  • tkinter = Tool to make windows, buttons, labels - Your UI. Built into Python, works on ANY PC, no OpenGL needed.
  • as tk = Short name. Instead of typing tkinter.Tk() every time, you can type tk.Tk() - short cut.

Line 5: from tkinter import filedialog

  • from ... import ... = From tkinter library, bring only one part called filedialog.
  • filedialog = The small window that opens when you click "Select file" - Shows your files to pick video.

Line 7: selected_file = ""

  • selected_file = Variable name you created. It will store path of video you select.
  • = = Assignment, give value.
  • "" = Empty string, means no file selected yet at start.

Line 9: def get_ffmpeg_path():

  • def = Define a function - You learned functions in Swaroop video.
  • get_ffmpeg_path = Name of function you created.
  • (): = Function takes no input, and : starts function body.

Line 10: if getattr(sys, '_MEIPASS', False):

  • if = If condition.
  • getattr = Check if something exists inside sys.
  • sys = System tool.
  • '_MEIPASS' = Secret folder PyInstaller creates inside .exe where it hides ffmpeg.exe. If this exists, means you are running as .exe app.
  • False = Default value if not found.

Line 11: return os.path.join(sys._MEIPASS, "ffmpeg.exe")

  • return = Give back value from function.
  • os.path.join = Join two paths correctly for Windows. Like C:\...\_MEIPASS + ffmpeg.exe = full path to ffmpeg inside .exe.
  • sys._MEIPASS = That secret folder.

Line 12: else:

  • else = If not running as .exe, do this.

Line 13: return "ffmpeg.exe"

  • Means ffmpeg.exe is in same folder as main_tk.py, like in your myfirstapp folder. For testing before making .exe.

Line 15: def select_video():

  • Function that runs when you click "Select Video" button.

Line 16: global selected_file

  • global = Use the variable selected_file that is outside function, not create new one inside. So file you select stays remembered for cutting.

Line 17: file = filedialog.askopenfilename(...)

  • file = New variable to store what user picked.
  • filedialog.askopenfilename = Open Windows file picker window.
  • filetypes=[...] = Show only video files in picker - *.mp4 *.avi *.mkv *.mov *.flv

Line 18: if file:

  • If user actually selected a file and didn't click Cancel.

Line 19: selected_file = file

  • Save selected path into global variable, so cut_video function can use it later.

Line 20: label.config(text=f"Selected: {os.path.basename(file)}")

  • label = Your text label at top of window.
  • .config = Change its settings.
  • text= = Change text shown.
  • f"..." = f-string, lets you put variable inside text.
  • os.path.basename(file) = From full path C:\Users\...\video.mp4, get only video.mp4 - Just file name, not full path.

Line 22: def cut_video():

  • Function that runs when you click "Cut 5 Seconds" button.

Line 23-26: Check if file selected

  • if not selected_file: = If still empty string, no video selected.
  • label.config(text="First select a video!") = Show message.
  • return = Stop function, don't continue.

Line 27: output = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(selected_file), "output_buddy.mp4")

  • output = Where new cut video will be saved.
  • os.path.dirname(selected_file) = Get folder of selected video.
  • os.path.join(..., "output_buddy.mp4") = Create new file path in same folder named output_buddy.mp4

Line 28: ffmpeg = get_ffmpeg_path()

  • Call your function from Line 9 to get correct path to ffmpeg.exe.

Line 29: command = f'{ffmpeg} -y -i "{selected_file}" -ss 00:00:02 -to 00:00:07 -c copy "{output}"'

  • command = Variable holding full FFmpeg command as text.
  • -y = Overwrite output if exists, don't ask.
  • -i "{selected_file}" = Input file, your selected video. Quotes " needed because path may have spaces like abcd PC.
  • -ss 00:00:02 -to 00:00:07 = Start at 2 sec, end at 7 sec = 5 sec cut - Same as you did in CMD!
  • -c copy = Don't re-encode, just copy - Fast, works on 1GB RAM.
  • "{output}" = Output file path.

Line 30: try:

  • Try to do something, if error happens, go to except.

Line 31: subprocess.run(command, shell=True, check=True)

  • subprocess.run = Actually RUN the FFmpeg command!
  • command = Your command text.
  • shell=True = Run through Windows shell.
  • check=True = If FFmpeg fails, raise error.

Line 32: label.config(text=f"Done! Created: {output}")

  • Show success message with output path.

Line 33: except Exception as e:

  • If error happens in try, catch it.
  • Exception as e = Store error details in variable e.

Line 34: label.config(text=f"Error: {e}")

  • Show error message.

Line 36-37: window = tk.Tk() etc.

  • tk.Tk() = Create main window object.
  • window.title(...) = Set title bar text to Buddy First Video Editor
  • window.geometry("500x300") = Window size 500 width, 300 height.

Line 39-40: Label

  • tk.Label = Text label widget.
  • window = Put it inside main window.
  • text=... = Initial text.
  • .pack(pady=20) = Place it in window with 20 pixels space above/below.

Line 42-46: Buttons

  • tk.Button = Button widget.
  • text="1. Select Video" = Text on button.
  • command=select_video = Which function to run when clicked - No ()! Just name.
  • pack(pady=10) = Place with 10 pixels gap.

Line 48: window.mainloop()

  • mainloop = Keep window open forever, waiting for button clicks. Without this, window would open and close instantly.

  4. Run python main_tk.py
  5. Window with 2 buttons will open!

Yes bro, you have many small typing mistakes - That's why Python will show red errors! Let me check line by line - You typed almost right, but small spelling mistakes matter a lot in Python!

Your Mistakes - I found 13 mistakes:

1. Line: if gettattr(says, '_MEIPASS',false):

  • You wrote: gettattr with 2 t's
  • Correct: getattr with 1 t only
  • You wrote: says
  • Correct: sys - s-y-s
  • You wrote: false small letters
  • Correct: False capital F - Python needs capital F!

2. Line: return.os.path.join(...)

  • You wrote: return.os - with dot after return
  • Correct: return os.path.join(...) - Space after return, no dot!
  • return is a separate word!

3. Line: return "ffmpeg"

  • You wrote: "ffmpeg" without .exe
  • Correct: "ffmpeg.exe" - Need .exe, otherwise Windows won't find it!

4. Line: filetypes=[("video files ", "*.mp4 *mkv *.avi *.mov *.flv")]

  • You wrote: *.mp4 *mkv - Second one missing dot! *mkv should be *.mkv
  • Correct: "*.mp4 *.mkv *.avi *.mov *.flv" - All need *. dot star!

5. Line: label.config(text=f"selected: { os.path.basenam(file)"})

  • 3 mistakes in one line!
  • You wrote: basenam - missing e at end
  • Correct: basename
  • You wrote: f"selected: { ... }" - You opened with " and also closed with " inside - Python gets confused!
  • Correct: Use different quotes: f'Selected: {os.path.basename(file)}' - Single quotes outside, or escape!
  • You wrote extra ) at end

6. Line: output = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(selected file), "output_buddy.mp4 ")

  • You wrote: selected file with space - Variable name cannot have space!
  • Correct: selected_file with underscore
  • You wrote: "output_buddy.mp4 " with space at end inside quotes - That space will become part of file name! File will be named output_buddy.mp4 with space!
  • Correct: "output_buddy.mp4" no space!

7. Line: command = f'{ffmpeg} -y -i "{selected file}" -ss 00:00:02 -to 00:00:08 -c copy "output" '

  • You wrote: "{selected file}" - Again space in variable name!
  • Correct: "{selected_file}" with underscore
  • You wrote: "output" - You wrote word output in quotes, not variable!
  • Correct: "{output}" - Variable output inside curly braces! And you need variable output not word "output"!
  • Your command says -to 00:00:08 - That's 6 seconds cut (2 to 8), not 5 seconds! If you want 5 seconds, use 00:00:07 - But 6 seconds is also okay!

8. Line: subprocess.run(comman, shell=true, check=true )

  • You wrote: comman - missing d!
  • Correct: command
  • You wrote: true small letters
  • Correct: True capital T - Python needs capital T!

9. Extra spaces:

  • You wrote subprocess with space, tk with space - Remove extra spaces, but Python will still work, just not clean!

Your Buddy firstvideoeditor.exe is 60MB with FFmpeg inside. It works on ANY PC - Vista to Win 11, 1GB to 16GB RAM, any iGPU.

Step 1: Upload to Google Drive

  1. Go to drive.google.com
  2. Upload Buddy firstvideoeditor.exe from dist folder
  3. Right click -> Share -> Anyone with link can view -> Copy link
  4. Now anyone with that link can download Buddy!

Step 2: Make it look professional - GitHub Releases [FREE - Best for developers]

  1. Create GitHub account - github.com
  2. Create new repository named Buddy-First-Video-Editor
  3. Go to Releases -> Create new release -> Upload your .exe file
  4. People can download from github.com/yourname/Buddy-First-Video-Editor/releases
  5. This is how real open-source editors like Shotcut, Kdenlive distribute!

Step 3: Make a simple website for Buddy [FREE]

  1. Go to sites.google.com or carrd.co
  2. Make one page: Buddy First Video Editor - Works on ANY PC - Windows Vista to 11, 1GB RAM
  3. Add button Download for Windows -> Link to your Google Drive or GitHub link
  4. Share that website link to friends, WhatsApp groups!

Problem you will face: When friends download, Windows SmartScreen and Avast will say "Unknown publisher" - Because your .exe is not signed. To fix, you need Code Signing Certificate - Costs $70 per year. But for now, friends can click "More info" -> "Run anyway" - All new developers face this!

WAY 2: For Mobile - Put on Google Play Store [Your original dream - Mobile first!]

Your current Buddy is PC version (Tkinter). For mobile, you need Kivy version + Buildozer.

Steps to put on Play Store:

  1. Build APK: You already learned Buildozer - Build Kivy version to APK
  2. Sign APK: Play Store needs signed APK. You need to create keystore file - One command: keytool -genkey... - I will give you when you build mobile version
  3. Create Google Play Console Account: Go to play.google.com/console - Pay $25 one time fee - Lifetime account
  4. Upload: Upload your signed APK, add screenshots, description "Buddy Video Editor - Works on any Android phone"
  5. Wait 2-3 days: Google reviews and publishes! Then anyone can search "Buddy Video Editor" on Play Store and install!

Cost: $25 one time.

For now, before Play Store, you can distribute APK directly:
Upload APK to Google Drive and share link - Friends can download APK and install - Like you installed your Hello app!

WAY 3: For Web - Make Buddy run in browser [ADVANCED - For future]

Your Tkinter app CANNOT run in browser directly - Tkinter is only for PC.

For web version, you need to rebuild using different tech:

  • Option A: Streamlit or Flask + FFmpeg.wasm - Your Python code runs on server, user uploads video on website, server cuts and gives output. Host on render.com or huggingface.co - FREE
  • Option B: CapCut style - 100% browser editing - Uses FFmpeg.wasm (FFmpeg inside browser). Very advanced, needs JavaScript.

For now, WAY 1 and WAY 2 are best for you!

Okay, GitHub is blocking click on Windows 7 old Chrome - This happens! Let's force it to click!

Try these 3 tricks - One will work:

Trick 1: Use Keyboard to Click

  1. Press Tab key many times on keyboard - Keep pressing Tab
  2. Each Tab will highlight different button on page
  3. Keep pressing Tab until the green Publish release button gets a blue border around it (focused)
  4. When it has blue border, press Enter key!

Trick 2: Remove Block with Inspect - Works 100%

  1. Right Click on green Publish release button -> Click Inspect or Inspect element
  2. A new window opens at bottom with code - Don't worry!
  3. You will see line like:
    <button ... disabled ...>Publish release</button>
  4. Double-click on word disabled and press Delete key to remove it!
  5. Then close that inspect window (X at top right of inspect window)
  6. Now click green Publish release button - It will work!

Trick 3: Use Different Browser

  1. You have blue e icon Edge browser on your taskbar (next to File Explorer)
  2. Open Edge
  3. Go to github.com/BuddyBoyKij999/Buddy-First-Video-Editor/releases
  4. Click on your draft -> Edit -> Publish release button will work in Edge!
